For one-dimensional linear regression the loss is
L(w, b) = 1/(2n) Σᵢ (yᵢ − (wxᵢ + b))²
The gradient of L with respect to w is:
options: A. (2/n)Σᵢ xᵢ(yᵢ−(wxᵢ+b))
B. −(1/n)Σᵢ xᵢ(yᵢ−(wxᵢ+b))
C. (1/n)Σᵢ (yᵢ−(wxᵢ+b))
D. −(2/n)Σᵢ xᵢ(yᵢ−(wxᵢ+b))
E. (1/n)Σᵢ xᵢ(yᵢ−(wxᵢ+b))

questions.text:
Let X be an n×d design matrix with n < d (more features than samples) and rank(X) = n.
Which statement is TRUE?
options: A. XᵀX is invertible, so ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy is the unique solution.
B. XᵀX is singular; infinitely many w fit the training data exactly, so ridge regularization or the pseudoinverse is needed.
C. The normal equation has no solution in this case.
D. The least-squares solution is unique because n equations determine d unknowns.
E. y must be centered to zero mean before the normal equation can be applied.
questions.correctAnswer: B. XᵀX is singular; infinitely many w fit the training data exactly, so ridge regularization or the pseudoinverse is needed.
questions.explanation: Rank(X^T X)=n<d, so it is singular. Full row rank makes every y attainable; the nullspace has dimension d-n. The pseudoinverse selects the minimum-norm fit, while ridge selects a regularized fit. These are ways to select a solution, not the only ways to find one.

questions.text:
With ridge-regularized loss J(w) = (1/n)‖Xw−y‖² + (λ/2)‖w‖²,
the vectorized gradient-descent update is:
options: A. w := w − α·(2/n)Xᵀ(Xw−y) + λw
B. w := w − α[(2/n)Xᵀ(Xw−y) + λw]
C. w := w − α[(1/n)Xᵀ(Xw−y) + (λ/2)w]
D. w := w + α[(2/n)Xᵀ(Xw−y) + λw]
E. w := w − α[(2/n)(Xw−y)Xᵀ + λw]
questions.explanation: The data gradient is (2/n)X^T(Xw-y); the penalty gradient is lambda*w. Gradient descent subtracts alpha times their sum.

questions.text:
For ridge regression ŵ_ridge = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy with λ > 0,
as λ → ∞:
options: A. ŵ_ridge approaches the zero vector.
B. ŵ_ridge approaches the ordinary least-squares solution.
C. the training error approaches zero.
D. the model becomes equivalent to k-nearest neighbors.
E. ‖ŵ_ridge‖ grows without bound.
questions.correctAnswer: A. ŵ_ridge approaches the zero vector.
questions.explanation: With every component of w penalized, (X^T X+lambda I)^-1 tends to zero as lambda tends to infinity, so the fitted weights tend to zero.

A model has 2% training error and 18% cross-validation error, and the validation curve
stays flat as the training size grows.
What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Add higher-degree polynomial features.
B. Decrease the regularization parameter λ.
C. Increase λ (or remove features) to reduce model complexity.
D. Collect twice as much training data.
E. Run gradient descent for more iterations.
questions.correctAnswer: C. Increase λ (or remove features) to reduce model complexity.
questions.explanation: Low training error and much larger validation error indicate high variance. Since the validation curve has plateaued, reducing complexity is the best listed intervention.

options: A. Pruning the tree with cost-complexity pruning.

questions.text: Which statement about the k-means algorithm is TRUE?
options: A. It always finds the globally optimal clustering.
B. The number of clusters k must be chosen in advance, and different random initializations can converge to different local optima.
C. It works well when clusters are elongated or non-spherical.

questions.correctAnswer: B. The number of clusters k must be chosen in advance, and different random initializations can converge to different local optima.

questions.text:
You fit a Gaussian to each feature for anomaly detection and pick the threshold ε by
maximizing F1 on a cross-validation set (flag x as anomaly if p(x) < ε).
If ε is set far too large, what happens?
options: A. Only the most extreme anomalies are flagged; recall collapses.
B. Many normal points are flagged as anomalies, so precision drops.
C. The fitted Gaussian parameters μ and σ² change.
D. Recall decreases while precision increases.
E. Nothing changes; ε only affects training time.
questions.correctAnswer: B. Many normal points are flagged as anomalies, so precision drops.
questions.explanation: Increasing epsilon expands the region p(x)<epsilon. Many normal points become false positives, typically reducing precision while increasing recall.

Consider a trained hard-margin support vector machine.
Removing which training points can change the learned decision boundary?
options: A. Only the support vectors.
B. All training points influence it equally.
C. Only the misclassified points.
D. No single training point can change it.
E. Only the points farthest from the boundary.
questions.explanation: Support vectors are the active margin constraints. Removing one can change the optimum; removing a non-support point leaves the optimum feasible. Not every support-vector removal must change it.

increasing γ typically:

B. makes the boundary more complex and localized; the risk of overfitting grows.

questions.correctAnswer: B. makes the boundary more complex and localized; the risk of overfitting grows.
questions.explanation: A larger gamma makes similarity decay over shorter distances, allowing a more localized and complex decision boundary.

Which statements about SVMs and kernels are TRUE?
options: A. The kernel trick computes inner products in the feature space without explicitly mapping the data.
B. The RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space.
C. Only the support vectors determine the SVM decision boundary.
D. SVMs are insensitive to feature scaling.
E. A linear kernel can separate every dataset that an RBF kernel can separate.
questions.explanation: Kernels supply implicit feature-space inner products; the RBF map is infinite dimensional. The SVM decision function uses nonzero dual coefficients at support vectors. Feature scales matter, and nonlinear separability need not imply linear separability.

Which statements about search algorithms are TRUE?
options: A. BFS is complete and optimal when all step costs are equal.
B. DFS uses O(bm) memory but is neither optimal nor complete in infinite spaces.
C. Uniform-cost search is optimal when all step costs are positive.
D. A* guarantees an optimal solution regardless of the heuristic used.
E. Greedy best-first search is optimal.
questions.explanation: Under the usual finite-branching assumptions BFS is complete and optimal for equal positive costs; DFS stores O(bm) frontier nodes and may follow an infinite branch. UCS is optimal when it returns a goal with positive costs; termination in infinite spaces additionally needs a positive lower bound on costs. A* needs appropriate heuristic conditions; greedy search is not generally optimal.

B. Item-based filtering is usually more scalable when users far outnumber items.
C. Collaborative filtering has no cold-start problem.
D. TF-IDF features of item descriptions can be used in content-based recommendation.

questions.explanation: User-based CF uses similar users. Item-based similarities can be cheaper when there are far fewer items than users. TF-IDF supports content matching. CF has cold-start issues; centering in Pearson correlation can change neighbor rankings relative to cosine.

Which statements about reinforcement learning are TRUE?

B. Q-learning is an off-policy temporal-difference method updating toward max_a Q(s′, a).
C. A discount factor γ close to 0 makes the agent far-sighted.
D. The Bellman optimality equation expresses V*(s) as the maximum expected return over actions.

questions.explanation: The exploitation branch is taken with probability 1-epsilon (random exploration can also choose the best action). Q-learning uses an off-policy max target. Bellman optimality maximizes expected return. Small gamma is short-sighted; more exploration is not always better.
